items.author: Salt Strong
items.excerpt: Discover the incredible impact of releasing a speckled trout over 20 inches and how one simple decision could help future fish populations.
items.search_text: Skip to content The Incredible Impact of Releasing ONE 20″+ Trout By: Joseph Simonds on October 8, 2026 Found In: Fishing Tips , Inshore Fishing , Salt Strong Podcast , Conservation Comments (13) What if releasing just ONE big speckled trout could help produce millions of future fish? Sounds pretty wild, right? Well, there’s some fascinating science behind it. I recently caught up with my buddy David Fladd, founder of Release Over 20 , to talk about what happens when we give bigger fish a chance to keep growing and spawning. And what started as a simple idea to protect trophy trout has turned into something MUCH bigger. Check out our conversation below! Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Learn More About Release Over 20 Why 20 Inches Matters Here’s something I didn’t know until I first met David several years ago. Most speckled trout over 20 inches are females. And those larger females play an incredibly important role in producing the next generation of fish. According to David, a 20-inch female trout can potentially produce around 20 MILLION eggs in a single spawning season! And here’s where it gets even more interesting. Unlike fish that spawn just once a year, speckled trout can spawn repeatedly throughout the warmer months. In fact, David explained that females may release portions of their eggs every four to five days during spawning season. And as those trout get bigger? Their egg production can increase dramatically. A 23- or 24-inch trout may produce considerably more eggs than a 20-inch fish. Now, that doesn’t mean every egg becomes another trout. Far from it. But when you consider how many eggs a single large female can produce, you start to see why giving some of those bigger fish another chance can make a difference. One fish today could potentially contribute to thousands of fish in the future. Pretty cool stuff! The Impact Is Already Adding Up Here’s where this story gets REALLY exciting. When David started Release Over 20, he wasn’t trying to create some massive conservation movement. He simply wanted to catch more big trout around Charleston, South Carolina. So he made a personal decision. Every speckled trout he caught over 20 inches was going back into the water. That was it. No new fishing regulations. No complicated rules. Just one angler making a choice to help improve his local fishery. Fast-forward to today, and thousands of anglers have joined the movement. During our conversation, David shared that more than 17,000 speckled trout over 20 inches had been recorded through the program. Using an estimated 20 million eggs per fish over one spawning season, that represents a theoretical spawning potential of approximately 345 BILLION eggs! Of course, that’s not a count of actual eggs produced or fish that survived. But it helps put the potential impact into perspective. And I’m especially proud of how our Salt Strong community has gotten involved. Multiple Salt Strong chapters are participating, and our Charleston chapter even earned recognition as the top organization in the program’s inaugural awards. Our St. Pete chapter had already surpassed its goal of 500 releases for 2026 when David and I recorded this conversation. That’s what I love about this whole thing. Anglers coming together to make fishing better for EVERYONE. It’s Bigger Than Speckled Trout While Release Over 20 started with speckled trout, David and his team have expanded the program to include five species: Speckled trout Redfish Flounder Sheepshead Striped bass And each species has its own interesting story. Take flounder, for example. David explained that male flounder generally don’t grow nearly as large as females. That means the keeper-sized flounder we’re catching in his region are overwhelmingly females. Pretty fascinating, right? Then there’s redfish. David and I discussed how protecting spawning fish can be especially important in areas where redfish populations have declined. And sometimes, helping those fish doesn’t necessarily mean releasing everything we catch. It might mean releasing a particularly large fish. Or giving spawning fish a break during certain times of the year. Or simply keeping a few fish for dinner instead of taking home a full limit. The goal isn’t to stop enjoying the fishery. It’s to help make sure there’s an abundance of fish to enjoy for years to come. And that’s something I think just about every angler can get behind. How YOU Can Get Involved One of the coolest things about Release Over 20 is how easy they’ve made it to participate. They’ve even turned conservation into a fun challenge with prizes! Here’s how it works: Download the FREE Release Over 20 app. Create your profile. Catch and release an eligible fish over 20 inches. Log your release in the app. Get entered for a chance to win fishing gear! That’s right. You can actually win tackle, hats, shirts, and other fishing goodies just for participating. The app doesn’t collect your GPS coordinates. You only need to provide the state where you caught and released the fish. David and his team are anglers, too. They understand how important it is to protect those hard-earned fishing spots! They’ve also created leaderboards for fishing clubs, organizations, and individual anglers. So if you’re part of a Salt Strong chapter, this is an awesome way to get everyone involved. Learn More About Release Over 20 Final Thoughts One thing I really appreciate about David is his approach to conservation. He’s not trying to tell everyone how they should fish. And neither am I. I love catching fish. I love eating fresh fish. And I love seeing families bring home a few fish for dinner. There’s absolutely nothing wrong with enjoying the harvest side of fishing within the regulations. But I also love the idea that one simple decision on the water could help create better fishing opportunities for our kids and grandkids. Imagine what our fisheries could look like if thousands of anglers made small decisions like that throughout the year. More fish. Bigger fish. And more incredible memories on the water. That’s a future worth working toward! So a HUGE shoutout to David Fladd and everyone involved with Release Over 20. Keep up the awesome work! And if you haven’t already, check out their free app and consider joining the movement. Now I’ve got a question for you… Do you have a personal size limit for releasing bigger trout, redfish, or other inshore species? Or have you participated in Release Over 20 already? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions Why should you release speckled trout over 20 inches? Larger speckled trout are often females capable of producing millions of eggs during spawning season. Releasing these fish gives them additional opportunities to reproduce and potentially contribute to future trout populations. How many eggs can a 20-inch speckled trout produce? According to David Fladd of Release Over 20, a 20-inch female speckled trout may produce approximately 20 million eggs over a spawning season. This is an estimate, not an exact number. Actual egg production varies based on factors such as the fish’s size, age, and reproductive condition. What species qualify for Release Over 20? Release Over 20 currently includes speckled trout, redfish, flounder, sheepshead, and striped bass. Anglers can record qualifying releases through the organization’s free app. Is the Release Over 20 app free? Yes! The Release Over 20 app is completely free. Anglers can record qualifying releases, participate in leaderboards, and receive entries into fishing gear giveaways. The app also protects your fishing spots by not collecting GPS coordinates. Does Release Over 20 mean you shouldn’t keep fish? Not at all! Release Over 20 encourages voluntary conservation and responsible fishing practices. Anglers can still enjoy keeping fish for dinner while making personal decisions about releasing larger fish that may be particularly valuable to future spawning populations. The goal is to help create healthier, more abundant fisheries for future generations. items.title: Quick Fall Fishing Lure Strategy: Know WHEN to Switch!
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Learn when to switch fall fishing lures! Coach Tony shares how to adjust your lure strategy based on feeding activity and water depth.
items.search_text:
Skip to content Quick Fall Fishing Lure Strategy: Know WHEN to Switch! By: Tony Acevedo on October 28, 2026 Found In: Fishing Tips , Inshore Fishing , Tackle & Gear , Artifical Lure Tips Comments (10) Fall is one of my FAVORITE times to get out on the water! But here’s the deal… As the water cools and baitfish start moving around, the fish aren’t always going to be feeding the same way. And if you’re throwing the wrong lure at the wrong time, you could be missing out on some BIG fish! In this quick video, I’ll show you how I adjust my lure strategy in the fall to stay on the bite! ﻿
Featured Gear Moonwalker Topwater Plug Skinny Lipper XL Prawn Shrimp Lure 5″ Mulligan Bomber Paddletail Ultimate Fall Lure Bundle (Free Skinny Lipper XL) 1. Start With WHERE the Fish Are Feeding Here’s something I always keep in mind when I’m fishing in the fall… Just because fish are feeding doesn’t mean they’re feeding on top! During those cooler early mornings, I love starting with a topwater like the Moonwalker when fish are actively feeding near the surface. There’s nothing quite like watching a redfish or trout come up and absolutely CRUSH a topwater plug! But what happens when you’re seeing baitfish getting chased and the topwater isn’t getting any love? That’s when I’ll switch things up. The Skinny Lipper XL is a great option when fish are chasing bigger baitfish just BELOW the surface. It creates plenty of action and commotion without requiring fish to come all the way up to eat. The lesson here? Don’t force a topwater bite if the fish are telling you something different! Pay attention to where the action is happening and adjust your presentation accordingly. 2. Know WHEN to Slow Things Down Not every fall fishing trip is going to be nonstop explosions and aggressive strikes. Sometimes the fish just aren’t in the mood to chase. And that’s when I see anglers make a BIG mistake… They keep working the same fast-moving lures, hoping something will eventually bite. Instead, I’ll slow things down and give those fish an easier meal. A shrimp imitation like the Prawn is one of my favorite ways to do that. I’ll work it around areas like: Grass edges Structure Deeper pockets Areas where fish can sit and ambush prey The goal is to keep that lure in the strike zone and give less aggressive fish an opportunity to eat. Remember, you don’t always need to change spots when the bite slows down. Sometimes you just need to change your presentation! 3. Match the Bigger Baitfish One of the things I love about fall fishing is the opportunity to target BIGGER predators feeding on larger baitfish. But just because there’s bigger bait around doesn’t mean you should blindly throw the biggest lure you’ve got. You still need to think about WHERE those fish are feeding. When I’m targeting bigger fish along drop-offs and deeper feeding zones, the 5″ Mulligan Bomber is a great option. That larger paddletail profile helps imitate bigger baitfish, and I can adjust how I’m fishing it based on the situation. And here’s something you don’t want to overlook… That same lure can work in the shallows, too! Rig it weedless, and you can fish shallower areas where predators may be hunting larger baitfish. The important thing is matching both the baitfish AND the depth where predators are feeding. Final Thoughts If there’s ONE thing I want you to take away from this quick lesson, it’s this: Fall fishing success isn’t just about WHAT lure you’re throwing. It’s knowing WHEN and WHERE to throw it! Pay attention to the baitfish, watch how predators are feeding, and don’t be afraid to switch things up. Those little adjustments can make a BIG difference in how many fish you catch! Now I’ve got a question for you… What’s your confidence lure when the fall bite starts heating up? Let me know in the comments below! Frequently Asked Questions What’s the best lure to throw for fall inshore fishing? There’s no single lure that’s best for every situation! I like having options that cover different depths and feeding behaviors. Topwaters, subsurface plugs, shrimp imitations, and paddletails all have their place depending on what the fish are doing. When should I switch from topwater to a subsurface lure? If I’m seeing fish chasing bait near the surface but they’re not committing to a topwater, that’s a good sign to try something just below the surface. A lure like the Skinny Lipper XL can be a great adjustment. What should I throw when fish aren’t aggressively feeding? That’s when I like slowing things down with a shrimp imitation like the Prawn. Working it around grass edges, structure, and deeper pockets can be effective when fish aren’t willing to chase faster-moving lures. Are bigger lures better for fall fishing? Not always! When larger baitfish are present, a bigger profile like the 5″ Mulligan Bomber can be a great match. But the key is still matching the forage and fishing the right depth, not simply throwing the biggest lure in your box. items.excerpt: Learn where to find tripletail and BIG bull redfish this fall! Luke shares proven fishing patterns, lure tips, and the best areas to target.
items.search_text: Skip to content Fall Fishing: How to Find Tripletail and BIG Redfish By: Joseph Simonds on October 15, 2026 Comments (14) Fall is one of the BEST times of year to fish, but there are a couple of opportunities that many anglers completely overlook. Luke just got back from an awesome tripletail fishing trip, and there’s a good reason these fish are showing up right now. But that’s not all… MASSIVE schools of big redfish are also moving into certain areas! In the video below, Luke and I break down two exciting fall fishing patterns, where to find these fish, and how to catch them. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Lure 1: Prawn XT Jr. (3.5″) Rigging: Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jighead Lure 2: Skinny Lipper XL Lure 3: Mulligan 5″ Bomber Crab Trap Buoys Are Fall Fishing GOLDMINES When crab trap buoys start appearing along the coast, it’s time to start looking for tripletail! Fall is Luke’s favorite season for targeting these fish, and the arrival of crab traps creates an incredible opportunity. Here’s why. Crab traps naturally attract smaller fish and other marine life, creating a steady source of food that draws in larger predators. Tripletail take advantage of this by positioning themselves underneath the floating buoys, where they can ambush unsuspecting prey. And they’re not limited to offshore waters! You can find tripletail around: Crab trap buoys in bays and nearshore waters. Channel markers and other floating structures. Buoys along beaches and coastal shorelines. Floating debris and vegetation. Luke has even encountered tripletail in water as shallow as TWO FEET! The key is to keep your eyes open. As you’re traveling between fishing spots, take a few extra minutes to inspect nearby buoys. Sometimes you’ll spot a fish immediately. Other times, you might check dozens of buoys before finding one. But when you do find one, the action can be incredible! The Biggest Mistake Anglers Make When Targeting Tripletail One of Luke’s biggest takeaways from years of targeting tripletail? DON’T overcomplicate it! Many anglers assume they need live shrimp or other live bait to consistently catch these fish. But Luke has found that a small artificial shrimp can be incredibly effective. His current favorite is the Prawn XT Jr. rigged on a jighead. And there’s an important reason he prefers this setup. Sink Rate Makes a HUGE Difference Tripletail frequently sit just beneath the surface, waiting to ambush anything that drifts into their feeding zone. To trigger a strike, Luke wants his lure to drop directly in front of the fish. He previously experimented with weedless hooks that allowed the lure to fall more slowly. The problem? His strike ratio dropped considerably! Switching to a jighead helped him get the lure into the strike zone much more effectively. For anglers concerned about snagging the buoy rope, Luke recommends using a weedless jighead, such as the Hoss Weedless Round Eye. The basic strategy is simple: Locate a tripletail hanging around a buoy or marker. Cast close enough to get the lure in front of the fish without snagging the rope. Allow the lure to drop naturally through its strike zone. Watch your line carefully for the strike! And don’t give up after one rejected presentation. Luke and Joe have encountered tripletail that refused numerous casts before finally deciding to eat. Persistence can pay off! Want BIG Bull Redfish? Stop Fishing ONLY the Shorelines! While tripletail are gathering around floating structure, another incredible fall fishing pattern is developing across expansive grass flats. Massive schools of oversized redfish are moving into the shallows! These aren’t your typical small schools of slot redfish. We’re talking about schools containing HUNDREDS of fish, including bull reds exceeding 36 inches! But here’s where many anglers go wrong. They spend all their time fishing docks, mangrove shorelines, and other obvious structure. Luke admits he made this same mistake for years. He was consistently fishing the shoreline while some of the biggest redfish were roaming the open flats behind him! Where to Find These Schools During the fall, Luke focuses on large, expansive grass flats located near major current flows. These areas can hold tremendous amounts of bait, including: Mullet Pinfish Shrimp Other small baitfish And when the bait concentrates, those big schools of redfish aren’t usually far behind. Luke particularly likes searching these areas early in the morning. Look for signs of life, including mullet schools, tailing redfish, or fish pushing water across the flats. The important thing to remember is that these fish MOVE! A school might be holding in one section of a grass flat today and roaming another section tomorrow. That’s why covering water is so important. Rather than spending your entire trip casting at shoreline structure, get out onto those expansive flats and actively search for feeding fish. You might be surprised at what you’ve been missing! The Right Lure Can Help You Find More Fish There’s another important difference between Luke’s tripletail and bull redfish strategies. For tripletail, he’s making accurate presentations to individual fish. But for schooling bull redfish, he’s trying to cover as much productive water as possible. That means switching to larger lures capable of making LONG casts. Two of his favorite options are: Skinny Lipper XL: A larger, shallow-running plug that casts extremely far and allows anglers to cover expansive flats. Mulligan 5″ Bomber: A larger paddletail that can help cover water while presenting a substantial baitfish profile. The advantage? These lures allow you to search water efficiently without constantly repositioning your boat. And when you finally locate a school of feeding redfish, things can get exciting FAST! With so many fish competing for food, one fish committing to your lure can trigger an incredible reaction from the rest of the school. Of course, the same grass flats can also hold excellent numbers of snook and speckled trout. Luke generally looks for snook closer to prominent shoreline points, oyster bars, and mangrove edges, while the larger redfish schools tend to roam more freely across the open flats. Find the food, and you’ll dramatically improve your chances of finding the fish! Final Thoughts There’s a reason Luke considers fall his FAVORITE time of year for inshore fishing. Between tripletail gathering around crab trap buoys, schools of bull redfish moving onto expansive flats, and excellent opportunities for snook and trout, there’s a LOT to get excited about! And in many areas, there’s another major advantage. LESS fishing pressure! With hunting season, football, and other fall activities keeping anglers off the water, you might find yourself enjoying some incredible fishing without the summer crowds. So if you’ve got a few extra hours to get on the water, TAKE ADVANTAGE! Have you been seeing tripletail around crab trap buoys or big schools of redfish in your area? Let us know where you’re fishing and what you’re catching in the comments below! Frequently Asked Questions When is the best time to catch tripletail? Fall is one of the best times to target tripletail, particularly as crab traps are deployed along the coast. Luke considers fall his favorite season for tripletail fishing, followed by spring. Where can you find tripletail in the fall? Tripletail frequently gather around crab trap buoys, channel markers, and floating debris. They can be found in bays, along beaches, and in nearshore waters at varying depths. What is the best artificial lure for tripletail? Luke recommends the Prawn XT Jr. rigged on a jighead. The realistic shrimp profile and controlled sink rate make it effective for presenting a lure directly in front of tripletail holding near floating structures. Where do big redfish schools go in the fall? Large schools of bull redfish frequently move onto expansive grass flats near major current flows and abundant baitfish populations. Look for mullet, surface disturbances, and other signs of feeding activity. What are the best lures for big redfish in the fall? Long-casting, shallow-running lures are excellent options for covering large grass flats. Luke recommends larger presentations such as the Skinny Lipper XL and Mulligan 5″ Bomber. items.title: EASIEST Way to Catch Mangrove Snapper (No Live Bait!)
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Learn how to catch mangrove snapper without live bait using one simple shrimp lure, shallow grass flats, and the right retrieve.
items.search_text: Skip to content EASIEST Way to Catch Mangrove Snapper (No Live Bait!) By: Luke Simonds on October 29, 2026 Found In: Fishing Tips , Inshore Fishing , Fishing Reports , Artifical Lure Tips Comments (21) Who says you need live bait to load up on mangrove snapper? On a recent trip to the Florida Keys, I decided to keep things simple. One shrimp lure, a basic inshore setup, and a few promising spots on the map. The result? I caught my limit of mangrove snapper before 9 AM! And here’s the really cool part… You don’t need to be in the Keys to put this strategy to work! In this video, I’ll show you exactly where I found the fish, how I worked my lure to get consistent bites, and a few simple tricks you can use to catch more fish on your next trip! Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Rod: Slot Machine 7’6″ Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Line: 10 lb J-Braid 8 Grand Leader: 20 Ib Ande Mono Lure: Prawn XT Jr Rigging Low Current: 3/0 Hoss Weedless Round Eye 1/4 oz Rigging High Current: 3/0 Hoss Weedless Round Eye 1/2 oz 1. Find the Potholes on Shallow Grass Flats When most anglers think about mangrove snapper, they picture fishing around bridges, docks, and deeper structure. But don’t overlook shallow grass flats! For this trip, I focused on sandy potholes surrounded by seagrass , especially areas with good current flow. These potholes create natural feeding opportunities where snapper and other predators can hang out and ambush prey. My strategy was simple: Find a productive stretch of grass flats with scattered potholes. Position up-current when possible. Cast into the potholes and work the lure along the bottom. Make a few casts before moving to the next one. When you find fish, slow down and thoroughly cover that area. And once I found one snapper, there were often more nearby! 2. One Shrimp Lure Was All I Needed I kept my setup about as simple as possible. My lure of choice was the Prawn XT Jr. rigged weedless on a 1/4 oz Hoss Round Eye Jighead. This combination allowed me to fish through the grass without constantly getting snagged while still dropping the lure into potholes several feet deep. The retrieve wasn’t complicated, either. I simply cast into the target area, let the shrimp sink toward the bottom, and worked it back with small hops and bumps. The key was keeping the lure near the bottom where the snapper were feeding. As the current picked up and I moved into a deeper channel, I switched to a 1/2 oz jighead to maintain better bottom contact. That small adjustment helped keep the bites coming! And the Prawn XT Jr. didn’t just catch mangrove snapper. I also hooked into mutton snapper and several other species throughout the trip. 3. Let the Current Help You Catch More Fish One of the biggest factors in this trip was how I positioned the boat relative to the current. Rather than randomly casting around the flat, I used the current and wind to quietly drift through productive areas. Whenever possible, I cast up-current and retrieved the shrimp back with the flow, letting it naturally bounce along the bottom. When I hooked a fish, I’d also make additional fan casts to see if more snapper were holding nearby. And when the current became too strong for the lighter jighead, adding weight allowed me to keep fishing effectively. The takeaway? Pay attention to current direction, keep your lure in the strike zone, and don’t be afraid to adjust your presentation. Those little details can make a BIG difference! Final Thoughts What I loved most about this trip was how simple everything was. No live bait. No complicated tackle. Just a shrimp lure, a basic inshore spinning combo, and some productive shallow-water structure. I even managed to catch my limit of mangrove snapper before 9 AM! And this isn’t just a Florida Keys strategy. The same approach to finding potholes, working current, and fishing a shrimp lure can be effective in shallow-water fisheries throughout the Southeast and Gulf Coast. Have you ever targeted mangrove snapper with artificial lures, or do you normally stick with live bait? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions Can you catch mangrove snapper without live bait? Absolutely! Artificial shrimp lures like the Prawn XT Jr. can be very effective, especially when worked near the bottom around productive structure and current. Where should I look for mangrove snapper on shallow flats? Look for sandy potholes surrounded by grass, particularly where there’s good current flow. These areas can hold surprising numbers of fish. What jighead weight works best for mangrove snapper? On this trip, I started with a 1/4 oz weedless jighead in shallow water and switched to a 1/2 oz jighead when stronger current made it difficult to maintain bottom contact. What’s the best retrieve for a shrimp lure? Start by allowing the lure to sink near the bottom, then work it back using small hops and bumps. Adjust your retrieve and weight based on current, depth, and where the fish are holding. items.title: Best & Worst Rigging Options for TPE & Plastisol Lures
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Learn which hooks and jigheads work best for TPE vs. plastisol soft plastic lures so you can rig them correctly and fish with confidence.
items.search_text: Skip to content Best & Worst Rigging Options for TPE & Plastisol Lures By: Luke Simonds on October 1, 2026 Found In: Fishing Tips , Inshore Fishing , Tackle & Gear , Artifical Lure Tips Comments (26) Give me 2 minutes, and I’ll make choosing the right jighead or weighted hook for your soft plastics a whole lot easier. I’ve tested more hook and jighead styles than I care to admit, and this quick breakdown covers the biggest lessons I learned through trial and error. By the end, you’ll know which keeper styles work best with different soft plastic materials so you can rig with more confidence, avoid bad combinations, and know exactly what to reach for next time. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Lures (Top to Bottom): Prawn Junior (original) Prawn XT Junior Featured Terminal Tackle (Top to Bottom): Hoss Helix Hook Hoss Screw Lock Jighead (coming soon) Hoss Round Eye Jighead Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jighead Hoss Prawn XT Jighead (coming soon) Z-Man Pro ShroomZ Jighead Z-Man Texas Eye Jighead TPE vs. Plastisol: Why Rigging Changes Most traditional soft plastic lures are made from plastisol. It’s soft, easy to work with, and usually rigs extremely well on corkscrew-style keepers. That’s why corkscrew weighted hooks and jigheads are some of my favorite options for plastisol lures. You can twist the lure onto the keeper, line everything up, and get a clean, secure presentation without much effort. TPE is a different story. TPE lures are MUCH tougher and stretchier. That durability is a huge advantage on the water. I fished the exact same Prawn XT for three days on a Louisiana trip and caught more than 60 fish on it. That same lure was still in great shape afterward, including both eyes. That’s pretty wild. But that same toughness can make TPE harder to rig on traditional corkscrew-style keepers. For TPE lures, I generally prefer a smaller hook-style keeper or a simpler keeper design that grabs the material without making you fight to twist or force it into place. The Simple Rule If you’re fishing plastisol , corkscrew-style keepers are usually an excellent choice. If you’re fishing TPE , smaller hook-style keepers are typically much easier to rig. There are exceptions, and most of these hooks can technically work with either material. But “can work” and “works well” are two different things. One Keeper Style I’d Be Careful With There’s also a popular keeper style that uses a larger horn or spike to hold the lure in place. That can work really well with certain materials, especially ElaZtech. But it’s not automatically a great fit for every soft plastic. On softer plastisol, that larger keeper can tear up the material. And on very tough TPE, getting the lure over a large keeper can be a pain. So the biggest takeaway is simple: Match your hook keeper to the MATERIAL of the lure, not just the lure size. Doing that makes rigging easier, helps the lure sit straighter, and can save you from wasting soft plastics or buying hook styles that don’t match what you fish. Final Thoughts The good news is that most weighted hooks and jigheads are still pretty interchangeable. You’re not totally locked into one style. But choosing the right keeper for the material makes a BIG difference. For plastisol, I generally like corkscrew-style keepers. For tough TPE lures, I’d lean toward smaller hook-style keepers that are easier to rig. That one little adjustment can save you a lot of frustration. What soft plastic and hook combination are you using right now? Let me know in the comments! FAQs What is the difference between TPE and plastisol soft plastic lures? Plastisol is the traditional soft plastic material used in many fishing lures. It’s soft, flexible, and easy to rig, but it can tear after repeated fish catches. TPE is much stretchier and more durable, which can help a lure last through a lot more fish. The tradeoff is that its toughness can make some hook keepers harder to rig. What hooks work best with TPE soft plastics? Hooks and jigheads with smaller, simpler keeper designs are usually easier to rig with TPE. Large corkscrews or keeper horns can be more difficult to twist or push into the tougher material. Are corkscrew hooks good for soft plastic lures? Yes. Corkscrew-style keepers work especially well with traditional plastisol soft plastics because the softer material twists onto the keeper easily and stays secure. Can you use the same jigheads for TPE and plastisol lures? In many cases, yes. But the keeper design can make one hook much easier to use with one material than another. Matching the keeper to the lure material will usually give you a cleaner rig and easier setup. Why are TPE fishing lures so durable? TPE is extremely elastic and resistant to tearing. That makes it much tougher than traditional plastisol and allows one lure to potentially survive dozens of fish catches. items.title: 6 Fishing Tackle Purchases We Regret Buying
items.author: Salt Strong
items.excerpt: Avoid fishing tackle purchases you’ll regret. We share six mistakes, what’s worth your money, and when cheaper gear is the better choice.
items.search_text: Skip to content 6 Fishing Tackle Purchases We Regret Buying By: Joseph Simonds on September 24, 2026 Found In: Fishing Tips , Inshore Fishing , Salt Strong Podcast , Tackle & Gear Comments (28) I spent $900 on a fishing reel… and I wish I could take it back. And Luke’s biggest regret? Something we STILL SELL. In this podcast, we’re sharing six tackle purchases we regret, so you know what to skip, what’s actually worth your money, and when the CHEAPER option is better. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Reel: Otis 2500 Lure 1: Mulligan 5-Inch Bomber Lure 2: Prawn Original Rod: Slot Machine I’ve owned a reel that cost around $900. It’s incredibly smooth, lightweight, and fun to fish with. But I started worrying about it so much that I didn’t want to travel with it or let my kids use it. That’s a lot of money tied up in something I’m sometimes afraid to enjoy. Luke made a different version of the same mistake: spending most of his budget on the reel, then buying a rod with whatever was left. For fishing with artificial lures, his priorities now are: Choose a rod suited to the fishing you’ll be doing. Pair it with quality line. Choose a reel that fits the rod and line. The rod affects your casting, your ability to feel a bite, and your hookset. It deserves more attention than the leftover budget. Luke now often spends at least twice as much on his rod as his reel. You don’t have to follow an exact ratio, but the point is worth remembering before you spend big on a reel. That’s also why we wanted the Otis 2500 to deliver the performance we need at a price that lets us enjoy using it. Buy Gear for the Fishing You Actually Do Years ago, I bought an expensive setup for a beach tarpon trip. I had one very specific situation in mind, went all in, and barely used that setup afterward. Then I made a similar mistake buying a dedicated live bait combo for an outing. The guide had gear available, and I could have used an inshore setup I already owned anyway. Before buying another rod and reel, ask yourself: How often will I actually use this? Can something I already own handle the job? Could I borrow the gear for this trip? Some situations call for specialized equipment. But buying a whole new setup for a single outing can leave you with an expensive reminder sitting in the corner. Be careful with combos that make the rod feel like a free bonus, too. A bargain loses its appeal when the rod doesn’t perform the way you need it to. Buy for the fishing you regularly do, and make sure the rod is right for the job. Choose Versatile Lures Before Fancy Colors It’s easy to look at a realistic paint job and think, “That HAS to catch fish.” Luke used to put a lot more value on those details. After years of testing, he cares much more about what a lure lets him do. Can he rig it weedless? Fish it shallow? Put it on a jighead and reach deeper water? That’s why he brought up the Prawn and Mulligan Bomber. With different rigging options, he can use those profiles across a range of depths and conditions without carrying a tackle bag full of specialized lures. Color can be part of the decision, but it shouldn’t distract you from getting your lure to the fish and presenting it effectively. Being good with a few versatile lures is more useful than owning every color of a lure you barely know how to fish. Focus on depth coverage, rigging, and learning how your lures work. A fancy paint job won’t do those things for you. Make Your Leader Earn the Extra Cost One of Luke’s biggest regrets was spending so much money on fluorocarbon leader. He believed the claims about its advantages. In fact, he started testing it because he expected to prove how good it was. His results changed his mind. In the comparisons he describes in this episode, regular monofilament performed better in abrasion testing, and he didn’t see a strike advantage from fluorocarbon when matching line diameters. That last detail matters: matching the pound-test rating isn’t necessarily the same as matching the diameter. Luke now uses mono for his inshore leaders based on those results and his experience landing fish. We sell both, but we’re going to share what we’ve found even when the less expensive option is the one we prefer. Before paying more for a leader, make sure the benefit you’re buying shows up in the fishing you do. Final Thoughts I’m all for buying good fishing gear. I just want it to earn its place on the boat. A rod that helps you fish better, a reel you enjoy using, and a few lures you know well can go a long way. The expensive setup collecting dust at home doesn’t help much. Now I want to hear yours. What’s a fishing purchase you regret, whether it didn’t work, wasn’t worth the money, or got used once and has been collecting dust ever since? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions Should I spend more on my rod or my reel? For the lure fishing we discuss here, Luke prioritizes the rod first, quality line second, and the reel third. Choose a rod suited to your fishing, then match the rest of the setup to it. Do I need a separate setup for live bait fishing? Not always. For the inshore live bait trip I describe, a setup I already owned would have handled the job. Consider the bait, target fish, and conditions before buying another combo. Does lure color matter more than depth? Luke puts more emphasis on depth coverage and presentation than exact color or realistic paint details. Start with a lure you can rig to reach the fish and work effectively. Which Mulligan lure does Luke mention? Luke discusses the 5-inch Mulligan Bomber . He highlights its versatility, including the ability to rig it weedless or use it on a jighead. Why does Luke prefer monofilament leader? In the testing and fishing experiences he describes, mono gave him better abrasion resistance without a noticeable reduction in strikes at comparable diameters. Those results led him to switch his inshore leaders to mono. items.title: 3 Essential Cut Bait Rigs for Shallow Water Inshore Fishing
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Learn 3 essential cut bait rigs for shallow water fishing, when to use each one, and how to avoid wasting bait in the wrong conditions.
items.search_text: Skip to content 3 Essential Cut Bait Rigs for Shallow Water Inshore Fishing By: Tony Acevedo on September 28, 2026 Found In: Fishing Tips , Inshore Fishing , Tackle & Gear Comments (43) Most anglers make cut bait WAY harder than it needs to be. In fact, 3 simple rigs will cover just about any shallow-water situation you’ll run into. But the rig is only HALF the equation. There’s one other detail that can mean the difference between quality fish and feeding catfish all day. Check out this video and you’ll be ready to catch more fish on cut bait the next time you hit the water. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Rod: Slam Stick Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Popping Cork Rig: Dr. Popper Freeline Rig: Gamakatsu Circle Hooks Leader: 20–30 lb Ande Mono Salt Strong Insiders can save 20% on eligible tackle at Fish Strong. 1. Freeline Rig: The Simple Go-To This is about as simple as cut bait fishing gets. Tie an inline circle hook to your leader, add your cut bait, and that’s it. No weight. This is the rig I use most often when fishing shallow, relatively clean water without a bunch of grass or structure along the bottom. Without a weight holding everything in place, your bait can naturally move with the wind and current. That’s a GOOD thing. Position yourself upwind or upcurrent from the area you want to target and let the bait slowly work toward it. Your bait moves naturally while its scent gets carried directly toward the fish. For most open-water situations, 20 lb monofilament leader is plenty. And make sure you’re using an inline circle hook , especially if you’re putting your rod in a rod holder and letting the fish hook itself. 2. Knocker Rig: When You Need More Control Take that same basic setup and add an egg sinker that can slide down your leader to the hook. Now you’ve got a knocker rig . This is the next rig I’ll reach for when the water gets a little deeper or the current gets strong enough that my bait won’t stay where I want it. For example, you might be fishing 3 to 4 feet of water and notice your freeline bait constantly rolling away from your target. That’s when some extra weight can help. The exact weight depends on the conditions. You don’t need to automatically grab the heaviest sinker in your tackle box. Use just enough weight to control your bait based on the depth and strength of the current. That keeps your bait in the strike zone without making the presentation unnecessarily heavy. 3. Popping Cork Rig: Grass, Structure & Dirty Water Sometimes you DON’T want your cut bait sitting on the bottom. Thick grass, oyster bars, and other structure can quickly bury your bait or leave you constantly snagged. A popping cork solves that problem by suspending your bait just above the structure. For this setup, I use a short section of 30 lb leader between my braid and the top of the cork. Below the cork, I’ll typically use 20 lb leader down to an inline circle hook. The length of that bottom leader depends on the depth and how high the grass or structure comes off the bottom. The goal is simple: Keep your bait right above it. There’s another advantage here, too. In dirty water, the popping cork creates additional sound as it moves around in the waves. That noise can get a fish’s attention before the scent of your cut bait helps close the deal. Where You Throw Cut Bait Matters MORE You can have the perfect cut bait rig and still waste an entire day. That’s because cut bait isn’t something you should randomly throw into the middle of a giant flat and hope a good fish eventually smells it. Instead, look for areas fish naturally use to travel and stage. One of my favorites is the edge of a flat where shallow water transitions into slightly deeper water. Those edges can act like highways for fish moving between feeding areas. Another great option is a deeper trough running alongside a shoreline. Pay attention to which direction the wind and current are moving. Position yourself so the scent from your bait travels through the area you’re trying to target. And don’t ignore points, oyster bars, and other staging areas connected to those travel routes. If a deeper trough leads toward a point, for example, fish can use that trough as a highway before stopping around the point to feed. Finally, look for life. Baitfish. Diving birds. Surface activity. Those clues can turn a massive stretch of water into a much smaller target zone. If you don’t get a bite after about 10 minutes, move down and try the next high-percentage area. You’re still covering water, just much slower than you would with artificial lures. Final Thoughts You don’t need a dozen complicated rigs to fish cut bait effectively. A freeline rig, knocker rig, and popping cork rig will cover the vast majority of shallow-water situations. The bigger key is knowing when to use each one and putting your bait somewhere quality fish are actually likely to travel or feed. That’s where planning your trip ahead of time can make a huge difference. If you need help identifying depth changes, points, structure, contours, and other high-percentage areas in your local waters, Smart Fishing Spots can help you narrow down where to start before you hit the water. Which of these three cut bait rigs do you use most often? Or do you have another way? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions What is the best cut bait rig for shallow water? A freeline rig with an inline circle hook is a great starting point when fishing shallow water with relatively clean bottom and manageable current. It allows your bait to move naturally with the water. When should I add weight to a cut bait rig? Add weight when stronger current or deeper water causes your bait to move too far from your target area. A simple knocker rig allows you to add enough weight to keep the bait under control. Should I use a circle hook for cut bait? Inline circle hooks are ideal for this style of fishing, especially when you’re placing the rod in a rod holder and allowing the fish to hook itself. Avoid offset circle hooks if your goal is to reduce the chance of deeply hooked fish. When should I use a popping cork with cut bait? Use a popping cork when fishing over grass, oyster bars, or other structure where you want to keep the bait suspended off the bottom. It can also provide additional sound and attraction in dirty water. Where should I throw cut bait? Focus on areas fish use as travel routes or staging areas, including flat edges, deeper shoreline troughs, points, oyster bars, and depth changes. Visible baitfish, birds, and other signs of feeding activity can help you narrow down the best places to fish. What can I use for cut bait? Mullet, ladyfish, pinfish, shrimp, and blue crab can all be used as cut bait. The best choice will depend on the forage available and the species you’re targeting.
